chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Abu al-Abbas, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

They brought to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) a short, ugly man whose belly was swollen with illness and the veins of his belly had turned around. He had committed fornication with a woman, so the woman said, 'I did not know of him except that he entered upon me.' The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said to him, 'Did you commit adultery?' He said, 'Yes,' and he was not married. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) raised his gaze and lowered it, then called for a palm branch, counted a hundred, and then whipped him with its stalks.
ai.seo_question: What was the punishment for an unmarried man who committed fornication according to this hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi illustrates the Prophet’s (peace be upon him and his family) judicial discretion in applying the hadd punishment of stoning or lashing, specifically noting the man's status as ghayr muhsan (unmarried) despite his physical infirmities. The use of a palm branch (‘idq) with its stalks (shamarikh) highlights the practical application of the prescribed hundred lashes, balancing the severity of the penalty with the individual's condition. It serves as a key precedent in Shia fiqh for understanding how physical ailments do not exempt one from the hadd of zina, provided the other conditions are met.
